tldr: Leveraging point-wise instantaneous Doppler velocity from FMCW Doppler LiDAR, this paper proposes an initialization framework that estimates pose, velocity, and IMU bias at an ultra-high frequency exceeding 10 kHz without relying on stationary states, specific excitation motions, or prior geometric map matching—even during violent motions or in degenerate environments like tunnels.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed Free-Init. The Doppler-Inertial Velocimeter (DIV) fuses point-wise Doppler velocity and angular velocity to update velocity and attitude at ultra-high frequency. Subsequent optimization estimates accelerometer bias and gravity, supplying reliable initial states and an undistorted static map to the downstream LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO).
overview:
LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) is vital for autonomous driving and robot navigation, but starting up poses a tough "initialization barrier." Conventional LIO assumes the robot begins completely stationary or performs specific excitation motions (shaking or wiggling) to estimate IMU biases and initial velocities. However, stationary assumptions fail for moving vehicles or fast-launching drones. Furthermore, inferring velocity from conventional LiDAR point clouds requires motion undistortion and geometric map correspondence (matching). This creates a chicken-and-egg dilemma: without position estimates, you cannot remove distortion, and without removing distortion, you cannot obtain a proper initial position.

To break this cycle, the authors focus on Doppler LiDAR using Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) technology. Beyond capturing 3D point coordinates, this LiDAR directly measures the Doppler velocity (relative line-of-sight velocity) along the laser beam for each point. Crucially, this velocity measurement is completely independent of the environment's geometry or the robot's current pose. Grounded in non-inertial kinematics, the authors design the Doppler-Inertial Velocimeter (DIV), which directly fuses point-wise Doppler velocity with gyroscope measurements. Updating via a Kalman filter as each individual point arrives enables accurate velocity and gyro bias estimation at an ultra-high frequency exceeding 10 kHz.

Experiments across diverse platforms—including handheld setups, wheeled robots, and an automobile traveling at 75 km/h—demonstrate that even under violent rotational and translational motions or inside featureless tunnels, Free-Init reliably completes high-precision initialization within seconds and without divergence, smoothly handing over stable initial states to downstream LIO systems.
contributions: Proposed Free-Init, a complete initialization framework for Doppler LiDAR-inertial systems that eliminates reliance on LiDAR scan undistortion, excitation motions, and map correspondences.
Designed the Doppler-Inertial Velocimeter (DIV), which exploits FMCW Doppler LiDAR properties to deliver ultra-high frequency outputs exceeding 10 kHz through point-wise filtering.
Formulated a unified Doppler observation model and an optimization problem for accelerometer bias and gravity vector estimation based on non-inertial kinematics.

Conducted extensive real-world experiments on handheld, wheeled, and vehicular platforms (up to 75 km/h) and in geometrically degenerate tunnel environments, validating successful initialization even from violent initial motions.

sections.heading: The Chicken-and-Egg Dilemma of Conventional Initialization and the Ideal Alternative
sections.summary: While online LIO requires accurate initial states, conventional methods assume stationary conditions or specific excitation motions, leaving them unable to handle in-motion startups or sudden aggressive maneuvers. Moreover, because conventional LiDAR relies on geometry, the initialization module itself depends on undistortion and map matching, making it inherently prone to divergence.
sections.details:
### Initialization in Existing LIO and Its Limits
Because online LiDAR-Inertial Odometry (LIO) relies on nonlinear estimators, it easily diverges if accurate initial attitude, velocity, and IMU biases are not provided at startup. However, most mainstream methods (such as FAST-LIO2) depend on a stationary assumption, requiring the robot to start completely at rest. Alternatively, they require external sensors like cameras or demand manual "excitation motions" that shake the system in specific patterns. For autonomous vehicles driving on highways or large drones already airborne, demanding a full stop or specific shaking motions at every startup is completely impractical.

### The Chicken-and-Egg Paradox of Geometric Correspondences
Conventional pulsed LiDAR only measures the range (geometry) of point clouds. Back-calculating velocity and bias from this requires motion undistortion during scanning and geometric correspondence (matching) against a partially built map. However, accurate geometric matching requires correct attitude and velocity, while obtaining correct attitude and velocity requires accurate geometric matching. When large errors exist in the initial state, distorted point clouds produce a distorted map, which feeds back to corrupt the estimator even further in a vicious cycle of errors.

### Breakthrough with Doppler LiDAR
The authors realized that FMCW (Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave) Doppler LiDAR can break this paradox. Thanks to the intrinsic Doppler effect, FMCW LiDAR captures not only the 3D position of each return point but also directly and instantaneously measures how fast that point moves relative to the sensor along the beam axis. This measurement is completely independent of surrounding geometry, historical maps, or the ego-vehicle pose estimate. Using this capability allows for an ideal initialization system that operates without any prior correspondences.

captions.F1: Mapping comparison when starting initialization while driving on a road. Default initialization (top) assumes a stationary state, causing the initial map to blur severely and diverge. In contrast, Free-Init (bottom) captures velocity accurately even in motion, producing a crisp map that clearly resolves poles and road signs.

sections.heading: Formulating Velocity and Acceleration via Non-Inertial Kinematics
sections.summary: Based on non-inertial kinematics, the authors formulate how velocities and accelerations transform between coordinate frames for a mobile robot with rigidly mounted, displaced LiDAR and IMU sensors. These first- and second-order kinematics serve as the foundation for subsequent velocity and accelerometer bias estimation.
sections.details:
### Frames and Notations
This paper defines the world frame (inertial frame) as $w$, the robot base frame (body frame, aligned with the IMU frame) as $b$, and the LiDAR frame as $l$. The initial body frame $b_0$ at system startup serves as the world frame $w$. Three-dimensional position vectors, linear velocities, and rotation matrices use explicit superscripts to strictly distinguish the frame of reference.

### Non-Inertial Kinematics
The LiDAR sensor and IMU are mounted at slightly displaced positions on a rigid body. In a non-inertial frame undergoing both rotation and translation, the LiDAR linear velocity $^{l}\mathbf{v}_{wl}$ is described by first-order non-inertial kinematics using the body linear velocity $^{b}\mathbf{v}_{wb}$, angular velocity $^{b}\bm{\omega}_{wb}$, and LiDAR-IMU extrinsic calibration parameters (position offset $^{b}\mathbf{p}_{bl}$ and rotation $\mathbf{R}_{bl}$):

$^{l}\mathbf{v}_{wl} = \mathbf{R}_{bl}^{\top} \left( {}^{b}\mathbf{v}_{wb} + \left[{}^{b}\bm{\omega}_{wb}\right]_{\times} {}^{b}\mathbf{p}_{bl} \right)$

where $\left[\cdot\right]_{\times}$ denotes the skew-symmetric matrix for cross products. Similarly, taking time derivatives yields the second-order kinematics relating accelerations. Thanks to these physical formulations, local velocity measurements captured by the LiDAR and angular velocities/accelerations sensed by the IMU can be coupled mathematically without inconsistencies.

sections.heading: The Core of Free-Init: Ultra-Fast Point-Wise Velocimeter and Gravity/Bias Optimization
sections.summary: Free-Init consists of two stages: the point-wise updated Doppler-Inertial Velocimeter (DIV) and an optimization problem that solves for gravity and accelerometer bias from accumulated data. By processing points one by one with a Kalman filter instead of waiting for a full scan, it achieves ultra-high frequency estimation exceeding 10 kHz with minimal latency.
sections.details:
### System State and DIV Design
The state vector estimated by the DIV is $\mathbf{x}_V \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$, comprising LiDAR linear velocity $^{l}\mathbf{v}_{wl}$, body linear velocity $^{b}\mathbf{v}_{wb}$, body angular velocity $^{b}\bm{\omega}_{wb}$, and gyroscope bias $^{b}\mathbf{b}_g$. State propagation uses a discrete-time model assuming a Gauss-Markov process.

### Point-Wise Doppler Velocity and Angular Velocity Measurement Updates
When a LiDAR point $p_j$ arrives, assuming it lies on a static object, the Doppler velocity measurement $\widetilde{v}^d_j$ is the inner product of the LiDAR velocity and the normalized direction vector $^{l_j}\mathbf{d}_{l_jp_j}$ toward the point. Combining this with the kinematics from Section II yields a linear observation model. Points on dynamic objects are discarded whenever their residuals exceed a threshold. Additionally, whenever an angular velocity reading arrives from the IMU, the state is updated using a gyro observation model. Because the DIV is formulated as a linear Kalman filter, computation is exceptionally lightweight. Updating point by point without waiting for scan completion allows the output rate to exceed 10 kHz.

### Pose Integration and Static Map Construction
Angular and linear velocities from the DIV are numerically integrated using high-accuracy schemes to recover the trajectory during initialization. Furthermore, using instantaneous poses, each point $p_j$ is immediately projected into the world frame, building an undistorted initial static map. Eliminating the need for separate scan undistortion routines is a major advantage.

### Optimization of Accelerometer Bias and Gravity
Using estimated velocities, attitudes, and accelerometer measurements accumulated during DIV execution, an optimization problem is solved via second-order kinematics to estimate accelerometer bias $^{b}\mathbf{b}_a$ and the gravity vector $^{w}\mathbf{g}$. Gravity is constrained to a 2D spherical manifold $\mathbb{S}^2$ with a magnitude of approximately 9.8 m/s$^2$. All estimated states, uncertainties (covariances), and the undistorted initial map are then handed over to the downstream LIO system (such as FAST-LIO2).

sections.heading: Real-World Experiments: Zero Failures Across Dynamic Starts, Violent Motions, and Tunnels
sections.summary: Dynamic startup experiments involving aggressive rotations and translations were carried out across three platforms: handheld, wheeled robot, and an automobile moving up to 75 km/h. While existing methods suffered initialization failures and divergence under harsh conditions, Free-Init successfully delivered highly accurate velocity estimation, trajectory recovery, and clear map reconstruction.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Benchmarking
A sensor setup using an Aeva Aeries II FMCW Doppler LiDAR and an Xsens IMU (200 Hz) was built, integrating Free-Init into both FAST-LIO2 (tightly coupled) and DLIO (loosely coupled). Baseline comparisons were made against each LIO's default initialization (stationary assumption). Ground truth was provided by an integrated RTK-GNSS/INS system.

### Localization Accuracy Under Dynamic Motion
In dynamic sequences involving violent rotations and translations during startup (dyna_01 to 06), default methods failed to estimate initial velocity; in dyna_02 and dyna_04, downstream LIO crashed (diverged) completely. Even in dyna_01, the default method suffered a large trajectory error of 6.65 m. In contrast, systems equipped with Free-Init absorbed initial errors immediately, keeping end-point errors upon returning to the start to just tens of centimeters, demonstrating outstanding accuracy (Table II). High-accuracy initialization was also achieved in vehicle sequences driving at 60 to 75 km/h (dyna_05, 06).

### Mapping Consistency and Behavior in Degenerate Environments
When starting during violent rotational motion, default initialization produced swirling, corrupted maps. Free-Init, on the other hand, immediately produced sharp maps with clearly distinguishable building outlines and pillars (Fig. F5).
Moreover, when initializing while moving forward inside a featureless straight tunnel (Fig. F6), the default method erroneously estimated that it was moving backward due to lack of geometric features and crashed. In contrast, Free-Init correctly and immediately estimated forward velocity from Doppler observations across handheld (~1.43 m/s), wheeled robot (~6.23 m/s), and vehicular (~16.88 m/s) tests, achieving stable startups throughout.

### Velocity Estimation Accuracy and Runtime
Comparing DIV velocity estimation errors against prior work by Yoon et al. showed that while the prior method experienced large error spikes exceeding 1.5 m/s right after startup, DIV converged rapidly with errors under 0.2 m/s from the very start (Fig. F7). Overall average execution time was exceptionally light, remaining well under 0.1 seconds (Table III).

captions.F5: Comparison of mapping results during initial startup: aggressively shaking while running handheld (top), sharp turns in a corridor (middle), and driving at 75 km/h (bottom). The default method (middle column) fails with messy, scattered point clouds, whereas Free-Init (right column) preserves clean and sharp environmental structures.
captions.F6: Initialization results while moving forward inside a geometrically degenerate tunnel. Across handheld (top), wheeled robot (middle), and vehicle (bottom), default initialization (right) falsely inferred backward motion and diverged, while Free-Init (middle) accurately captured the true forward velocities (1.43, 6.23, and 16.88 m/s).
captions.F7: Velocity estimation error over time in vehicle driving datasets (dyna_05, dyna_06). Prior work (Yoon et al. 2023, green/magenta) exhibits significant velocity spikes early on, whereas the proposed DIV (blue/red) maintains remarkably low errors and high stability from the moment of startup.

sections.heading: How Doppler LiDAR Paves the Way for Fully Autonomous Robots
sections.summary: Free-Init establishes an innovative initialization framework free from dependencies on scans, specific motions, and geometric correspondences. Resolving intrinsic Doppler velocity measurements through first-order kinematics represents an impactful advance that extends beyond initialization to kidnapped-robot recovery and aggressive motion control.
sections.details:
### Significance of the Results
By formulating the physical advantages of FMCW Doppler LiDAR (point-wise instantaneous velocity sensing) within elegant non-inertial kinematics, Free-Init fundamentally eliminates the long-standing initialization bottleneck in LIO. Requiring no stationary rest, prior maps, or pre-startup shaking motions means systems can start anytime and anywhere, dramatically improving real-world robot reliability.

### Future Outlook and Applications
The authors highlight that this breakthrough extends far beyond an initialization module for LIO. For instance, online re-initialization during kidnapped robot scenarios where a platform is abruptly relocated, 10 kHz feedback velocimeters for drones performing aggressive aerobatics, and multi-session map merging during long-distance driving all stand to benefit enormously from directly perceiving velocity.

takeaways: Line-of-sight velocity from FMCW Doppler LiDAR is an absolute observation independent of maps or ego-pose, fundamentally resolving the chicken-and-egg dilemma of initialization.
Employing a point-wise discrete-time Kalman filter enables ultra-high frequency velocity estimation exceeding 10 kHz without waiting for full scan accumulation or performing complex undistortion.
In geometrically degenerate environments such as tunnels and straight roads, Doppler velocity prevents divergence caused by false geometric motion estimates.
The framework is highly practical and plug-and-play compatible with mainstream LIO systems such as FAST-LIO2 and DLIO.
limitations: During the dynamic initialization phase using only FMCW Doppler LiDAR and gyroscopes, gyro bias observability is relatively weak from a system identification standpoint, which may necessitate reliance on pre-calibration values or constant approximations.
Dynamic object rejection relies on a simple residual thresholding heuristic, requiring caution in extreme environments where large moving obstacles dominate the initialization field of view.

FMCW Doppler LiDAR hardware remains more expensive and bulkier than traditional pulsed LiDAR, meaning widespread adoption on compact drones depends on future hardware miniaturization and cost reductions.
